title: 11+ Grammar School vs Independent School Entrance: How Preparation Differs
description: Grammar and independent-school 11+ tests can differ significantly. Learn what to check about target schools, subjects, formats, timing and interview stages.

children: “11+” is a useful label, but it does not describe one national examination. Grammar-school selection arrangements vary by area and consortium, while independent schools may use their own papers, shared assessment providers, pre-tests, interviews or combinations of these. Preparation should therefore begin with the target school or local process, not with a generic 11+ workbook.
The first task: build a target-school map

Before deciding what to teach, parents should collect the current admissions information for each realistic target school. School websites and official admissions information should take priority over old forum posts or second-hand descriptions because formats can change.
Which schools are genuinely being considered?
What is the application and test timeline?
Which subjects or reasoning components are assessed?
Is there a named test provider, consortium or school-written paper?
Are there separate stages such as a second paper or interview?
What sample or familiarisation material does the school publish?
Grammar-school preparation

Grammar-school entrance tests are commonly designed to rank a large number of candidates against a defined selection process. Speed, accuracy and familiarity with the relevant question formats can therefore matter alongside underlying English and maths knowledge. The exact mix varies by area, so practice should mirror the actual local assessment only after the fundamentals are secure.

A child who is weak in comprehension or arithmetic does not solve that problem simply by completing more timed papers. Early preparation should repair the underlying skill; timed and format-specific practice becomes more useful once the foundations are stable.
Independent-school preparation

Independent-school entry can be more varied. Some schools use established assessment providers, some use their own English and maths papers, and some include interviews or additional stages. Written responses may demand more extended reasoning or expression than a highly standardised multiple-choice test. Again, the school’s current information should determine the plan.
Where an interview matters, preparation should help a child think aloud, discuss interests, justify opinions and respond thoughtfully. It should not manufacture a rehearsed personality.
What is shared across both routes?
Secure reading comprehension and vocabulary.
Accurate arithmetic and confident mathematical reasoning.
The ability to infer, justify and check rather than guess.
Enough timed practice to make the real assessment feel familiar.
A calm routine that protects sleep, schoolwork and motivation.
When should preparation become test-specific?

There is no single correct starting age. A sensible sequence is foundations first, targeted gap-filling next, then increasing familiarity with the real format as the assessment approaches. Starting earlier does not automatically mean doing more papers; it should often mean improving reading, number fluency and reasoning without turning childhood into continuous test preparation.
A useful parent checklist
Target schools confirmed.
Official admissions pages bookmarked.
Current test components checked.
Dates and registration requirements recorded.
Recent schoolwork or baseline evidence available.
Strengths and weaknesses identified.
A realistic weekly practice routine agreed.
What good 11+ tuition should do

Good tuition should make the plan more specific over time. It should be able to explain why a particular task is being used, how it connects to the target assessment, what the child is learning from mistakes, and when support can be reduced. It should also be willing to say when a generic exercise is not relevant to the school being targeted.
